Keyword extractors tell you what a document is about. Term extractors tell you what a domain is made of. A survey of the ATE literature — from the 1998 C-value algorithm to 2025 LLM prompting — with a working Python implementation, benchmark results, and a decision guide
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Automatic Term Extraction (ATE): Mapping the domain vocabularySearch for “keyword extraction in Python” and you will find hundreds of tutorials: TF-IDF with scikit-learn, RAKE, YAKE, TextRank, KeyBERT. Search for “automatic term extraction” and you will find almost nothing outside the academic literature — where the task has a formal definition, a manually annotated multilingual benchmark, three survey papers published between 2023 and 2026, and an active research frontier.
This asymmetry is unfortunate, because the two tasks are not the same, and the harder one is better studied. Automatic Term Extraction (ATE) is, in the words of the field’s most recent survey, “a Natural Language Processing (NLP) task intended to automatically identify specialized terms present in domain-specific corpora,” where terms function “as units of knowledge in a specific field of expertise” (Tran et al., 2026). The output is not a per-document summary; it is a termbase — the vocabulary that constitutes a domain.
This article surveys the field and implements it. We derive the C-value algorithm from first principles, build a complete extraction pipeline in dependency-free Python, run it on a wind-energy corpus, and then subject the output to an honest error analysis. We then trace what the research literature has established since: the ACTER benchmark that made ATE systems comparable, the Transformer models that displaced feature engineering, and the recent and genuinely nuanced findings about where large language models help and where they do not.
Principal findings:

• Terms and keywords answer different questions; conflating them produces systems that optimise the wrong objective.

• The C-value algorithm (Frantzi et al., 2000) remains in use in 50% of published ATE studies, twenty-five years after its introduction (Blandón Andrade et al., 2026).

• Transformer token classification is the current state of the art, reaching 58.3–69.6 F1 on the ACTER benchmark against 54.2–66.1 for the best feature-engineered system (Tran et al., 2023).

• LLM in-context learning matches fine-tuned encoders under domain shift (60.2 vs. 61.2 F1) but trails them badly in-domain (53.8 vs. 88.5 F1) (Chun et al., 2025).

• The nested-term problem, diagnosed in 1998, remains an open challenge for neural systems in 2026.
▶ Run the code while you read. Every pipeline stage in this article is worked through cell by cell in the companion notebook: Automatic Term Extraction from Scratch on Kaggle · source on GitHub. The tables and figures below are its actual output.

1. Terms Are Not Keywords
The distinction is not pedantic; it determines the entire system design.
Keyword extraction operates on a single document and asks: which words best summarise this text? The reference point is the document itself. TF-IDF answers it by contrasting the document against the rest of the collection; KeyBERT answers it by measuring the cosine similarity between candidate phrases and the document embedding. Both are, structurally, summarisation signals.
Term extraction operates on a domain corpus and asks: which expressions constitute the specialised vocabulary of this field? The reference point is general language. A term such as doubly fed induction generator is a term regardless of which wind-energy document it appears in, and regardless of whether it summarises that document.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Table 1. Synthesis by the author, drawing on Tran et al. (2023) and Rigouts Terryn et al. (2020) for the ATE column.The consequences are concrete. A TF-IDF pipeline over a unigram vocabulary cannot, in principle, emit doubly fed induction generator as a single unit. A KeyBERT ranking will favour phrases that summarise a document over phrases that define a field. Neither models the relationship between wind farm and offshore wind farm.
1.1 What counts as a term?
The question resists a purely theoretical answer, which is why the ACTER annotation scheme is valuable: it operationalises the definition into categories that human annotators can apply consistently (Rigouts Terryn et al., 2020).
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Table 2. Source: Rigouts Terryn, Hoste, Drouin & Lefever (2020), TermEval 2020, COMPUTERM @ LREC 2020, pp. 85–94.This four-way split explains a convention that otherwise looks arbitrary in the literature: ATE papers report two sets of scores, one for terms only and one for terms plus named entities. Named-entity recognition and term extraction overlap without coinciding, and the benchmark refuses to pretend otherwise.

2. The Canonical Pipeline
Nearly all classical ATE systems share a two-stage architecture: a linguistic filter that proposes syntactically plausible candidates, followed by statistical ranking that scores them. The systematic literature mapping of Blandón Andrade et al. (2026) found this hybrid design in 50% of the 113 papers they reviewed, against 38.2% purely statistical and 11.8% purely linguistic.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Figure 1. Pipeline after Frantzi et al. (2000); adoption statistic from Blandón Andrade et al. (2026).The ranking stage is conventionally decomposed into two distinct properties:

• Unithood — is this sequence of words a coherent lexical unit, or an accidental collocation?

• Termhood — assuming it is a unit, is it specific to this domain, or general language?
C-value addresses unithood. Weirdness and TF-IDF address termhood. Systems that measure only one produce characteristic failures: unithood alone accepts frequent but general phrases; termhood alone accepts fragments of terms.

3. Stage One: The Linguistic Filter
Frantzi et al. (2000) restrict candidates to part-of-speech patterns, offering three filters of increasing permissiveness:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima (2000), International Journal on Digital Libraries 3(2), 115–130.The choice is a precision/recall dial. The closed filter yields fewer, cleaner candidates; the open filter captures prepositional terms such as quality of service at the cost of substantial noise.
For a dependency-free implementation we approximate the POS filter with a stopword-boundary chunker, which exploits the fact that English terms rarely span a function word. Within each stopword-free chunk of a sentence, every n-gram up to length four becomes a candidate:
def candidates(text, min_len=1, max_len=4):
"""Inside each stopword-free chunk of a sentence, emit every n-gram."""
out = []
for sentence in SENT_SPLIT_RE.split(text):
chunk = []
for token in tokenize(sentence) + [None]: # None flushes the chunk
if token is None or token in STOPWORDS or len(token) < 3:
for n in range(min_len, max_len + 1):
for i in range(len(chunk) - n + 1):
out.append(tuple(chunk[i:i + n]))
chunk = []
else:
chunk.append(token)
return outThis is the same candidate-generation strategy RAKE uses. The difference between RAKE and ATE lies entirely in what happens next.

4. Stage Two: C-value and the Nested-Term Problem
4.1 The problem
Raw frequency systematically over-ranks substrings. If offshore wind farm occurs twice, then wind farm necessarily occurs at least twice as well, and a frequency-ranked list will credit the shorter string with occurrences it never independently earned. Frantzi et al. (2000) named these nested terms and designed C-value specifically to handle them.
4.2 The formula
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima (2000), International Journal on Digital Libraries 3(2), 115–130.Source: Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima (2000), International Journal on Digital Libraries 3(2), 115–130.Three mechanisms operate simultaneously. The log₂|a| factor rewards length, encoding the empirical observation that multi-word expressions are more likely to be terms than single words. The f(a) term preserves frequency as evidence. The subtraction removes the frequency that a merely inherited from longer terms containing it — the average frequency of every longer candidate in which a is nested.
4.3 Implementation
def c_value(freqs, min_freq=2):
longer_containing = defaultdict(list)
by_len = defaultdict(list)
for cand in freqs:
by_len[len(cand)].append(cand) for length, shorter_list in by_len.items():
for shorter in shorter_list:
for longer_len in range(length + 1, MAX_LEN + 1):
for longer in by_len.get(longer_len, ()):
if _contains(longer, shorter):
longer_containing[shorter].append(freqs[longer]) scores = {}
for cand, freq in freqs.items():
if freq < min_freq:
continue
length_weight = math.log2(len(cand)) if len(cand) > 1 else 0.5
nested_in = longer_containing.get(cand)
if nested_in:
score = length_weight * (freq - sum(nested_in) / len(nested_in))
else:
score = length_weight * freq
if score > 0:
scores[cand] = score
return scores4.4 The correction, observed
Running this on the wind-energy corpus makes the mechanism visible.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Figure 2. Computed in the companion notebook; C-value after Frantzi et al. (2000).Consider the three candidates wind farm, offshore wind farm and axis wind. All three occur; frequency alone ranks wind farm (f = 5) far above the others. C-value redistributes the evidence: wind farm retains a score of 3.86 rather than 5, because two of its five occurrences were inside offshore wind farm. Meanwhile axis wind — which in this corpus appears almost exclusively inside axis wind turbine — is discounted from f = 2 to a C-value of 0.75, and falls to the bottom of the ranking. The algorithm has, without supervision, distinguished an independent term from a fragment.
4.5 NC-value: the context extension
Frantzi et al. extend C-value with context evidence. Term context words are learned from the top-ranked candidates and weighted by the proportion of candidate terms they co-occur with, and the final score combines the two sources of evidence:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima (2000), International Journal on Digital Libraries 3(2), 115–130.Here t(w) is the number of candidate terms that context word w appears with, n the total number of candidates considered, Cₐ the set of distinct context words of a, and f_a(b) the frequency of b as a context word of a.
The hand-tuned 0.8/0.2 weighting is a period detail worth noting: it illustrates how differently NLP systems were constructed before end-to-end learning.

5. Stage Three: Termhood via Contrastive Scoring
C-value measures unithood but is blind to domain specificity. A phrase can be a perfectly coherent unit and still be general language. The standard remedy is weirdness (Ahmad et al.), which contrasts the technical corpus against a general-language reference:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Source: Ahmad, Gillam & Tostevin — weirdness / corpus-comparison indexing.def weirdness(tech_tokens, general_tokens, smoothing=0.5):
f_tech, f_gen = Counter(tech_tokens), Counter(general_tokens)
n_tech, n_gen = max(len(tech_tokens), 1), max(len(general_tokens), 1)
return {
w: (f / n_tech) / ((f_gen[w] + smoothing) / n_gen)
for w, f in f_tech.items()
}For multi-word candidates the word-level scores are aggregated by geometric mean, so that a single anomalous word cannot carry an entire phrase. The final termhood score combines both dimensions, with a logarithmic dampener so that weirdness re-ranks rather than dominates:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Combination used by the companion notebook; not taken from a published system.termhood = c_value_score * math.log1p(weirdness_score)Plotting the two axes against each other shows t
